name: Sam Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork improver for Ardent Formwork, subcontracted on a nine-storey hotel in the city centre. Formwork is the wooden and steel moulds you build so the concrete can be poured into the right shape. I spend my day building column boxes and deck shutters, striking them after the pour, cleaning and oiling the panels, and slinging loads to the tower crane. It's heavy and it's loud, but there's a good bunch of lads and the money's steady while the frame's going up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside the site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Leah, who's a receptionist at a dental practice, booking appointments and answering phones all day. We rent a flat near the ring road and we're saving for a deposit, about four months of money put by right now. I left school at sixteen, did warehouse work, then got on site through a mate. I use AI now and then, like when Leah got it to fix my CV, but I'm not on it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped. On site I'd say what everyone says, that you can't pour concrete with a chatbot. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. Construction's busy around here, there are cranes all over the city. My problem is just learning the trade properly so I'm not the junior forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd ask the foreman to put me on setting out with the chain gang, the lads who mark where columns go, so I pick that up. And keep the deposit money growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty normal, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the hotel frame is finished?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ardent moves us to the next job, usually. There's a car park and a student block lined up next year. If Ardent ever runs dry, there are four other formwork firms in this city who'd take a lad who turns up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How's the deposit going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. Rent eats a lot. We're at about nine grand, and we need maybe twenty for the kind of place we want, so another two or three years if nothing goes wrong.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, fair enough, and leave it there.
I'd tell the lads you **can't pour concrete** with a chatbot.
think: Construction is **busy** around here, with cranes all over the city.
My real problem is **learning the trade** so I'm not junior forever.
do: Ask the foreman for time on **setting out** with the engineers.
Keep adding to the **deposit savings** each month.
S0.quote: If Ardent ever runs dry, there are four other formwork firms in this city who'd take a lad who turns up on time.
fieldNote: He feels secure because **local demand** for formwork is strong.
His goal is a **house deposit**, about nine grand of twenty saved.
He wants to move up via **setting out**, a slightly more technical skill.

steps.text: Ask the foreman for time learning setting out
Keep putting money into the house deposit each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trades are fine and the office jobs need to watch out. I'd probably say it a bit carefully, though, because of Leah. I'd say people should get help to move jobs if theirs goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much yet. The site managers will use AI for programmes and orders, and maybe that means fewer engineers in the cabin. But the formwork's still built by hand, for now. It's Leah's job I'm thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get her to look at something more hands-on, maybe dental nursing, which she's mentioned. I'd keep saving but slower, because we might need it to cover her training. And I'd try the app the site uses for daily reports, once the other lads have figured it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Fine for me, not fine for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Leah answers phones and books appointments. Where does she fit in this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Leah books appointments and answers phones all day, and that's the exact list of jobs this AI is meant to take. The practice manager already put in an online booking system last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you two cut first if her hours went down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit plan, sadly. We'd put the house off two years and keep renting. Holidays would go too, and the car would have to last.

say: I'd say **office jobs** need to watch out more than the trades.
I'd say people should get **help to move jobs** if theirs goes.
think: The **site cabin** might shrink as managers use AI for programmes.
**Leah's job** is the one I'm worried about, not mine.
do: Encourage Leah to look at **dental nursing** training.
Slow the deposit saving to cover **her training costs**.
Try the site's **daily reports app** after others have.
feel: He feels **uneasy**: fine for himself, not for the household.
S1.quote: My partner Leah books appointments and answers phones all day, and that's the exact list of jobs this AI is meant to take.
fieldNote: The household risk sits with **Leah's receptionist job**, high on thinking AI.
His own day is **hands-on**, so he places himself later in the queue.
The **house deposit** is the first thing they'd delay.

steps.text: Help Leah apply for a dental nursing course
Try the site's daily reports app once others use it
Put the house deposit plan back two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast and the government needs to catch people. Proper support, not just benefits. I'd say it calmly though, I'm not a shouter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means Leah's out of work by 2028 and I'm out by 2031 or 2032. Robots that can build a column box and strike it would kill formwork labour. The engineers and planners go first, then us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the house and keep the money as a cushion. Leah would retrain straight away, maybe nursing or care. I'd try to get qualified as a crane slinger and signaller, because someone has to supervise lifts, and I'd look at moving to a smaller town where old buildings need work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor has gone soft under us both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leah the night you both realised what was happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leah (his partner) that the house can wait, and that the only thing that matters is one of us still having a wage in 2031. And then probably we'd just sit there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the site look like in 2031 in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Formwork that's mostly steel panels, put up by machines and checked by a camera. Maybe one or two people watching. I'm not sure which two, and I'm not sure I'd be one of them.

say: I'd say this is **too fast**, and government needs to catch people.
I'd want **proper support**, not just benefits.
think: Leah's out by **2028**, and I'm out by 2031 or 2032.
Robots that build and strike **column boxes** would end formwork labour.
do: Stop the **house deposit** and keep it as a cushion.
Get qualified as a **crane slinger and signaller**.
Look at moving to a **smaller town** with older buildings.
feel: He feels **alarmed**, like the floor has gone soft under them both.
S2.quote: I'd tell Leah (his partner) that the house can wait, and that the only thing that matters is one of us still having a wage in 2031.
fieldNote: Both household earners are hit, Leah at **2028** and Sam three years later.
His hands-on work only buys a **three-year delay**, which he says plainly.
Priority shifts from a deposit to **keeping one wage**.

steps.text: Freeze the house deposit and keep it as an emergency fund
Take the crane slinger and signaller qualification
Look at moving to a smaller town with old buildings
Help Leah start nursing or care training straight away

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, but not loads. People should start moving now. I'd probably say it to the lads at break more than anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means Leah's got time to train before 2031, and I've got till about 2034. That's enough for me to get the slinger ticket and maybe move into something like site safety, where you need a person signing off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Leah to start dental nursing this year, part time while she keeps her receptionist job. I'd do the slinger and signaller course next spring. We'd keep saving, but put the deposit plan back a bit to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. More like nervous than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the five years change what Leah does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, but smaller. A small flat with a mortgage we can pay on one wage beats a nice house we lose in 2034. That's how I'd think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still try to buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd go part time on reception and train as a dental nurse, which means hands in mouths, not booking. It's not robot-proof forever, but it buys years.

say: I'd say there's **time**, but not loads of it.
I'd tell the lads at break to **start moving now** on new skills.
think: Leah can **train before 2031**, and I've got till about 2034.
I could move into **site safety**, where a person still signs off.
do: Help Leah start **dental nursing** part time this year.
Take the **slinger and signaller** course next spring.
Aim for a smaller flat payable on **one wage**.
feel: He feels **anxious** but with a plan, more nervous than scared.
S3.quote: A small flat with a mortgage we can pay on one wage beats a nice house we lose in 2034.
fieldNote: Five years gives the couple a **two-step plan**: Leah first, then Sam.
He reframes the house goal around **one wage**.
**Site safety** appeals because it needs a person signing off.

steps.text: Help Leah start part-time dental nurse training this year
Take the slinger and signaller course next spring
Keep saving for a smaller flat payable on one wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you're sensible. I'd tell people to learn something extra and not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is fine for me. I'd be properly skilled, maybe a chargehand, before the robots turn up around 2039. Leah's the one with the clock, but even she's got years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, just keep going on formwork and buy the house as planned. Leah would start looking at dental nursing courses. I'd do a safety course in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly calm. It's far enough off that it doesn't spoil the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house, a chargehand job, Leah in a job she likes. By 2036 I'd want a mortgage half paid off, so a robot turning up on site isn't the end of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about the long version that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting lazy, like all of us. Plus not knowing what the robots would actually do. Nobody really knows, so you're planning in the fog a bit.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if you're sensible.
I'd tell people to **learn something extra** and not to panic.
think: I'd be a **chargehand** before robots arrive around 2039.
**Leah's job** has the shorter clock, but she still has years.
do: Keep doing formwork and **buy the house** as planned.
Take a **site safety course** in a couple of years.
feel: He feels **mostly calm**, with a little unease.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'd want a mortgage half paid off, so a robot turning up on site isn't the end of the house.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets him **keep the house plan**.
He still carries a low worry because **Leah's job** is exposed earlier.
He admits he's **planning in fog** about what robots will do.

steps.text: Keep working formwork and buy the house as planned
Pay extra into the mortgage before robots reach site

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits both of us. My partner Leah loses her job first, then I lose mine, and the house we were saving for turns into the money we live on. Help paying for Leah to retrain would be the big thing, and some kind of support while we both switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples. Everyone asks about one person's job, but it's the two wages together that pay the rent. If one goes, the other one's plans go too.

headlineQuote: My partner Leah loses her job first, then I lose mine, and the house we were saving for turns into the money we live on.
portrait: Sam is a 27-year-old **formwork improver** on a city-centre hotel frame.
He lives with **Leah**, a dental receptionist, and they're saving for a **house deposit**.
He's **pragmatic**, open to change once proven, and uses AI only now and then.
His worry is the **household**: Leah's job is exposed years before his.
With ten years, he keeps the **house plan**; with two, it becomes their emergency fund.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when Leah loses her job first and his follows by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Help paying for **Leah to retrain**, and support while they both switch.
